blocks.text: Demand
Macro backdrop

blocks.html: The macro frame for travel demand is one of slow but positive growth, with little change month-over-month. Barclays’ economists forecast global GDP running at 2.3–3.4% saar per quarter through 3Q27, with the US revised up (2.5% in 3Q26, ~2.0% through 2027) and the euro area anaemic — broadly 0.9–1.1% saar from 4Q26 through 2Q27 after a 2.6% print in 2Q26 — with France and Italy capped under 1ppt through 2Q27 and Germany brightening into 2027. GS’s read is consistent: Europe real GDP is expected to average ~0.9% and US ~2.0% over the next four quarters. On the leading indicators GS tracks for aircraft orders, the July US ISM sat slightly above its historical average while China PMI remained slightly below its long-term average. Nothing in the macro data argues for a demand-side break; the pressure on the industry this year is a cost shock, not an income shock.

blocks.text: Global passenger traffic

blocks.html: The demand picture softened through 1H26 but did not break. IATA's June update cut its full-year 2026 traffic growth forecast from +4.9% to +2.1%, and year-to-date global RPK growth through July was running at just +0.6%. The monthly cadence has nevertheless been improving: GS forecasts that IATA will report July traffic up 2.4% yoy with a global load factor of 85%, while Barclays’ read of the published IATA series shows industry traffic recovering to roughly flat yoy in July as the Middle East recovers, with Europe up 2%. The three July readings are differently constructed rather than contradictory — GS is forecasting the IATA print from individual airline reports and TSA volumes, Barclays tracks the published IATA series, and the IATA YTD figure averages the weak conflict months — but the spread illustrates how noisy single-month demand data currently is. We standardise on the IATA release as the reference series for this tracker.

blocks.html: Capacity is the other half of the load-factor story. Global airline forward scheduled capacity shows yoy growth of just +2/+3/+3% for August, September and October — which GS characterises as disciplined expansion and a modest stabilisation following the fuel-driven slowdown — while JPM notes capacity worldwide has been cut versus entering-the-year plans specifically to prop up fares against higher fuel. In other words, record load factors are being engineered through restraint on frequency, not carried by accelerating volume; that restraint supports fares and lessee cash flow, but it also means utilisation of the in-service fleet, rather than fleet growth, is doing the work.

blocks.text: US demand

blocks.html: The US is the firmest major demand pocket in the dataset — and it is pricing-led, not volume-led. Volumes are near-flat: North America RPKs were up just +1.0% yoy in May (IATA, Exhibit 2), the slowest growth of any region outside the Middle East collapse, and Barclays notes TSA international travel volumes are now falling yoy — the basis for its view that RASK will evolve weaker than fares as loads fade. Pricing is carrying the P&L instead: US airline yields were up 6.7% yoy in 1Q26 per GS, and on the transatlantic — the premium long-haul market that matters most for US network carriers — Barclays’ August screen-scrape has American’s economy fares +32% yoy, United’s +26% and Delta’s in the +10–20% band. The backdrop supports it: Barclays revised US GDP up to 2.5% saar for 3Q26 and ~2.0% through 2027 (Exhibit 1), and GS’s high-end corroborator — US business jet operations — was up 7% yoy in July after +5% in June. For the Fund, this two-speed US market maps directly onto the book: the fare strength accrues to network carriers with transatlantic exposure — United, the book’s Tier-1 anchor at ~25% of lessee exposure including the monetised JOLCO aircraft — while the soft end sits in domestic leisure LCCs, where the Fund’s one such position, ex-Spirit, has already been realised at 2.11x gross MoM.

blocks.text: European airline pricing & consumer demand

blocks.html: Barclays’ August screen-scraped fare data shows the post-conflict fare support cracking on short-haul: every European full-service carrier tracked was down yoy on intra-Europe fares — Austrian –1%, Brussels –2%, Lufthansa and SWISS –3%, Aer Lingus and Iberia –4%, TAP, KLM, Aegean and Air France down mid-single digits, with British Airways –11% and Finnair –18% the weakest. The LCC picture is mixed: Vueling +5%, Eurowings +4% and Transavia France +4% were up, while Wizz –11%, Ryanair –10%, Norwegian –9%, TUI –8% and Jet2 –5% were lower. Barclays itself cautions that the screen-scraping rests on booking-curve assumptions — direction credible, scale less so — and notes the Ryanair reading is weaker than the company’s own ~–2% guidance for the quarter, with both Ryanair and Wizz flagging that September data was brightening. Long-haul is the offset: North Atlantic economy fares remain strong, led by Brussels +43%, British Airways +37%, Swiss +29% and Austrian +28%, with only Aer Lingus (–2%) and TAP (–8%) down. At group level the split is stark: Lufthansa Group –2% short-haul vs +22% North Atlantic, AF-KLM –6% vs +6%, IAG –8% vs +21%.

blocks.html: Consumer spending corroborates the stabilisation. Barclays’ proprietary UK card data puts spending on airlines at –1.6% yoy over the 28 days through 11 September — little changed from –1.5% in the prior edition but a material improvement from –10% yoy in June, which Barclays attributes to a later booking pattern for peak-summer travel this year. The recovery is broad-based across age groups, though the youngest cohorts (–10.1% yoy) continue to lag older travellers (+10.9%), and airline spend as a share of total card spend is running a touch below 2025 YTD. For a lessor book this matters mainly through the lessee P&L: European short-haul operators — the natural home of mid-life narrowbody aircraft — are facing softening yields into a high fuel-cost winter, while long-haul widebody operators retain pricing power.

blocks.text: Airline profitability & fuel

blocks.html: Profitability is where the conflict bites. IATA’s post-conflict forecast puts 2026 industry net profit at US$23bn on a 2.0% net margin — roughly half the US$41bn / 3.9% it projected in December 2025 before the conflict — with jet fuel assumed to average US$152/bbl for the full year versus US$90/bbl in 2025, lifting the industry fuel bill to US$350bn. Demand fundamentals stay intact: IATA still expects a record 84.0% load factor for 2026, up from 83.5% in 2025. Record load factors alongside collapsing margins frame this as a cost shock to airline P&Ls rather than a demand shock to aircraft. JPM makes the same point from the credit side: US$23bn is still a healthy absolute figure — if an anaemic return on the capital employed to generate it — and most airlines under its coverage are holding up well, especially those focused on premium, international and loyalty revenue.

blocks.html: The open question is whether the fuel assumption holds. JPM notes NY Harbor jet fuel has risen over 136% YTD, from ~US$2.00/gal at end-2025 to above US$4.70/gal in mid-September — well above the run-rate implied by IATA’s US$152/bbl (≈US$3.62/gal) full-year average — with fuel representing 15–30% of airline operating expenses. Forward curves imply lower fuel costs, and GS observes crude and jet fuel prices are already off their recent highs. Either spot follows the curve down in 4Q26, or IATA’s profit forecast gets cut a third time.

blocks.text: Supply
Order backlog & deliveries

blocks.html: The order book remains the structural anchor: IATA counted more than 18,000 aircraft on order as of May 2026, over half the active global fleet. Monthly order flow stayed healthy through the conflict — Boeing booked 38 gross orders against 8 cancellations in July and Airbus 204 against 1 — with GS characterising net orders as consistent with prior mid-cycle periods, order campaigning activity as robust for both growth and replacement, and cancellations as a share of backlog as below historical averages. Parked aircraft stood at 11.1% of the total fleet in July, down 40bp month-over-month and nearing pre-pandemic levels — the clearest single indicator that the usable surplus in the system is thin.

blocks.text: Supply normalisation watch

blocks.html: The more important development is the direction of travel. JPM argues the supply-demand imbalance that defined the post-COVID market is normalising: OEM production rates are rising (MAX 7/10 certification expected this year, 777X next year), the GTF engine overhaul queue is shrinking, and the Spirit liquidation and Air Baltic fleet reduction are returning aircraft to the market. The depressed retirement rate — which has pushed lease renewal rates from a typical 50–60% to often above 80% across many portfolios — is expected to normalise as OEM supply recovers, whether or not fuel recedes. Higher fuel itself cuts both ways for fleets: all else equal it raises demand for newer, fuel-efficient aircraft and lowers demand for older, less efficient models, though JPM stresses that six months of elevated fuel does not materially alter fleet plans when the futures curve implies lower costs ahead. None of this is distress: JPM frames it as an industry “playing from a position of strength”, with the secondary trading market arguably the strongest it has ever been. But it marks a turn in the cycle narrative that the record-backlog headline alone does not capture.

Values & Lease Rates
Aircraft values & lease rates by segment

blocks.html: Appraiser data now shows the first clear bifurcation of the cycle. Per IBA (as cited by JPM), 10-year-old widebody values are up sharply — the 777-300ER roughly +40% yoy and the A330-300 roughly +15% — on persistent scarcity and delayed fleet renewal, while 10-year-old A320-200 and 737-800 values both fell marginally QoQ and yoy, the first outright declines in older narrowbody values this cycle. Market lease rates show the same split: A320-200 rates down 13.0% yoy and 737-800 down 11%, against roughly +20% for the 777-300ER. New-delivery values and lease rates remain far less volatile, and because new lease rates are indexed to interest rates they are under upward pressure — the 10yr UST is +80bp YTD, approaching 5% — even as new narrowbody lease rate factors compress with normalising supply. The appraiser consensus JPM describes is of slightly weakening mid-life lease rates concentrated on the single-aisle side, with the twin-aisle runway for lease rate improvement remaining longer.

blocks.text: Lessor portfolio economics

blocks.html: Portfolio-level economics are still improving on the strength of leases written into the shortage, and Avolon’s 2Q26 results are the cleanest read. Its CFO put the portfolio lease rate factor at 10.4%, “a nudge below what it peaked at pre-COVID”, with lease yields up 20bp yoy from 10.2%, and management stating it continues to place aircraft at the highest lease rates it has seen in years. 2Q26 net income was US$209mm, up 45% yoy, bringing trailing 12-month net income to US$702mm, up 31% yoy — “almost back to peak profitability levels back in the 2018–2019 range” per the CFO — and management continues to believe the persistent OEM production delays at Airbus and Boeing will support the sector through the end of the decade (all per JPM’s 2Q26 recap). Across JPM’s comps, LTM lease yields run from 8.6% (SMBC Aviation Capital) to 12.7% (BOC Aviation) — see Exhibit 9 — with the spread largely a function of fleet age and funding mix rather than underwriting. On the origination side, sale-leasebacks represented ~31% of total 2025 deliveries per Cirium (via GS), keeping competition for new-delivery deals intense.

Financing & Credit
Lessor credit & relative value

blocks.html: The ratings catch-up trade is over. AerCap now carries Baa1/BBB+ and AVOL, ACGCAP, AYR and DUBAEE have reached mid-BBB; JPM’s view is that most of the expected upgrades have played out and the market is now “fighting for a few basis points here and there in a compressed spread market”. On relative value, 5yr AER trades ~5bp wide of the GSIB cohort (versus ~20bp when JPM downgraded the name in August 2024), offers ~35bp over NSC 5yr green bonds (49bp) and ~20bp over CP and FDX (5yr FDX at 64bp), while the most recent AAL first-lien EETC trades just inside 100bp — lessors screen a touch cheap versus other equipment lessors and transports, but rich versus GSIBs, which JPM regards as the floor on further spread compression outside a true financial crisis.

blocks.text: Funding & maturity profile

blocks.html: Funding markets remain wide open for the rated lessors, and the model keeps shifting unsecured. Avolon — which runs the largest order book in the space and is among the most active public issuers — ended 2Q26 with an unsecured debt / total debt ratio of 79%, up from 77% at year-end 2025, issued US$1.5bn of senior unsecured notes during 1H26, upsized a revolver by US$175mm to a US$6.38bn commitment, and generated US$2.4bn of LTM operating cash flow, with JPM also noting a wide-open unsecured bank market (all per JPM’s 2Q26 recap).

The 2027 towers are concentrated at SMBCAC (US$5.3bn) and SUMIAL (US$5.0bn), with AER carrying the single largest 2028 load (US$6.1bn). None of this is a solvency question for investment-grade issuers in an open market — but it anchors why new-delivery lease rates, indexed to funding costs, stay under upward pressure, and why cost of debt is the competitive variable among origination platforms.

blocks.text: Five observations we consider important after reading this quarter’s materials, ordered by importance:

blocks.html: 1. GP and sell-side cycle narratives have diverged. The GP’s letter leans on the record backlog and supply scarcity; JPM’s same-quarter judgment is that the imbalance “is or will normalise”, with retirements picking up and lease renewal rates mean-reverting from 80%+ toward the typical 50–60%. Both can be true — the backlog is a stock, supply recovery is a flow — but the flow is what prices mid-life aircraft, and the fund’s two portfolio acquisitions are weighted to A320ceo / 737NG vintages that sit exactly where IBA records the first value declines of this cycle. The pace and pricing of the in-progress monetisations is the practical test; we will track the GP’s supply language each quarter as the leading indicator.

The September NY Harbor spot above US$4.70/gal runs ~30% above the rate implied by IATA’s US$152/bbl full-year average (≈US$3.62/gal): either 4Q fuel follows the futures curve down, or IATA cuts industry profits a third time. blocks.html: The Fund has sourced five transactions to date; pro forma for monetisations executed and in progress it holds 29x aircraft and 5x engines. The current portfolio stands at US$1,352M on a purchase-price basis against the US$3,750M scaled target (36%, up from US$1,245M / ~33% at Q1 2026). Concentration sits in the two newest transactions — Portfolio Acquisition #2 (14x aircraft, 40% of current portfolio value) and VietJet (6x 737-8 delivering July–November 2026, 32%) — followed by United (19%), Portfolio Acquisition #1 (6%) and the Rolls-Royce engine pool (3%); the Fund holds minority equity allocations in the two opportunistic pools (~19% of the 9-aircraft 2025 pool and ~23% of the engine pool) alongside the platform. blocks.text: DPI vs fund age: platform pacing against the aviation base rate

blocks.html: Placing every fund on a DPI-versus-age axis (first-investment basis) gives the aviation analogue of the PE report’s quartile-curve exhibit — with the realised peers standing in for a benchmark curve that does not exist for this asset class. The base rate is slow: the fully-realised peers took 7–14 years to reach 0.54–1.33x DPI. Against that, Griffin Vintage 1’s 0.76x at age ~5 is within two points of Falko I’s full-life 0.78x reached at age ~11, and Vintage 2’s 0.51x at age ~4 matches the Investec debt fund’s 0.54x at age ~12 — the platform is distributing at roughly twice the pace of the reporting base rate, consistent with its securitisation- and JOLCO-led monetisation model. BCGAF at 0.05x / age ~1 sits where an early-life fund should; the pacing question becomes testable from 2027. Caveats run in both directions: Griffin DPI is GP-reported on a gross-invested-capital denominator versus PitchBook’s contributions basis, the reporting peer set is small and survivor-tilted, and monetisation-led DPI recycles asset value rather than harvesting lease yield — the same “engineered versus exit-driven distributions” caveat the PE report applies to GPS V.

Against that, Griffin Vintage 1’s 0.76x at age ~5 is within two points of Falko I’s full-life 0.78x reached at age ~11, and Vintage 2’s 0.51x at age ~4 matches the Investec debt fund’s 0.54x at age ~12 — the platform is distributing at roughly twice the pace of the reporting base rate, consistent with its securitisation- and JOLCO-led monetisation model. BCGAF at 0.05x / age ~1 sits where an early-life fund should; the pacing question becomes testable from 2027. Caveats run in both directions: Griffin DPI is GP-reported on a gross-invested-capital denominator versus PitchBook’s contributions basis, the reporting peer set is small and survivor-tilted, and monetisation-led DPI recycles asset value rather than harvesting lease yield — the same “engineered versus exit-driven distributions” caveat the PE report applies to GPS V.

blocks.text: Deployment pace

blocks.html: The one genuine QoQ-capable comparison available before fund-level performance prints is deployment pace — and it cuts both ways. BCGAF has called 36.0% of commitments at age ~1, against Castlelake Aviation V Stable Yield’s 28.3% at age ~3 (per PitchBook), with the portfolio at 36% of its US$3,750M scaled target within five quarters of initial close. Fast deployment into a cycle the market section describes as normalising — supply recovering, first value declines printing in 10-year A320ceo/737NG metal — is vintage-concentration risk: the capital is being put to work fastest exactly where the fund’s two portfolio acquisitions sit. The mitigants are the GP’s 5–10% purchase-price discounts (scorecard: meeting target), the staged VietJet deliveries through 2H26, and the fact that it is simultaneously selling into the same bid at 1.40–2.95x monetisation marks — a two-sided book rather than a one-way ramp. The called-percentage series for BCGAF and the live peers starts in the ledger this quarter; pace divergence becomes a tracked QoQ item from 2026Q4.

ABS funding cost league

blocks.html: Funding cost is the competitive variable the market section flags on the liability side, and aviation ABS pricing is public — so this module tracks it deal by deal. The trend into the conflict was steady compression: senior lease-ABS spreads went from T+205bp at the 2024 reopening (AASET 2024-1) to +160–180bp through 2025 and +145bp by February 2026 (CLAS 2026-1), with aviation loan ABS printing the floor at +105bp AAA (PKAIR 2026-1) and Merit’s March deal achieving what bank reports called the second-lowest Class A spread in aviation ABS/CLO history. The Iran-war escalation in late February paused the lease market for ~7 weeks; Castlelake’s CLAS 2026-2 reopened it in April, and by Sky’s SLAM 2026-1 — the eighth aviation lease ABS of 2026 and third post-conflict — five-month issuance was running roughly double 2025’s pace (per Ishka). For the Fund specifically: Griffin’s inaugural Master Trust series (Nov-25, US$1,245M) was the largest aircraft ABS ever issued, and its measurable efficiency is in the advance rate — a 77.6% senior LTV at single-A versus 69–75% on the discrete-trust peers — paired with 14-year mortgage-style amortisation that matches aircraft depreciation. The June 2026 US$568M second series, which carries the Fund’s Q1-acquired aircraft, priced with spreads tightening versus the inaugural per Ishka’s report; the exact level is not yet publicly disclosed and populates from the presale next quarter. The allocator read: cheap senior funding is available to every scaled platform (Castlelake alone has raised ~US$8.6bn of ABS debt since inception, per KBRA), so market access per se is not differentiation — the edge shows in advance rate and master-trust re-issuance speed, and the same spread compression that funds the GP’s pipeline is what is compressing the new-delivery lease rate factors on the asset side.

blocks.html: This is the first quarter recorded in the aviation competitor ledger, so — as in the Private Credit and PE reports’ inaugural runs — this module records levels rather than quarter-on-quarter change, and the series becomes genuine momentum from next quarter by appending to the ledger. With BCGAF itself not meaningful, the baseline percentile reading uses the Griffin platform vintages as proxy, on the strict-below convention (share of the reporting cohort strictly below the subject, subject excluded; TVPI cohort n=5): Vintage 2’s 1.6x net MoM baselines at the 100th percentile and Vintage 1’s 1.4x at the 80th — with the usual caveat that the GP’s gross-invested-capital MoM is not identical to PitchBook TVPI. BCGAF enters the percentile series the quarter its own fund-level metrics print; the practical trigger to watch is PitchBook back-filling its row, which today still shows a stale US$30M fund size against the actual US$353.0M. Baseline levels, peer rows and methodology are archived in av_comp_series_2026Q3.json alongside the source screen for next quarter’s delta computation.

Appendix — peer universe and methodology

blocks.html: The current screen holds 17 vehicles of which 5 report performance — but it is a keyword screen (“aircraft”, all investors) and therefore under-captures the true universe: Carlyle Aviation’s SASOF III–VI, Castlelake’s flagship Aviation IV/V, Sky Leasing and the transport-ABF sleeves at ITE and others typically carry no “aircraft” in the fund name (the screen’s Sciens ASOF II is the SASOF lineage’s predecessor), and PitchBook strategy tags are unreliable in this niche — Castlelake V Stable Yield, a leasing vehicle, is tagged “distressed debt” — so strategy-filter screens misfire too. An investor-based re-pull (Carlyle Aviation Partners / Castlelake / Sky Leasing / Falko / Napier Park / ITE / Bain Capital, unioned with keywords) is the planned refresh; the fund-formation-by-vintage exhibit is deferred to that re-pull, since charting the keyword sample would mislead. On fundraising competition, the visible points are Castlelake’s US$2bn raised for V Stable Yield (2023 vintage) and BCGAF’s US$353.0M raising toward a US$1bn target into an October 2026 final close. Methodology: vintages follow PitchBook’s first-investment convention throughout; percentile = share of the reporting cohort strictly below the subject, subject excluded; manager-reported and PitchBook figures are shown side by side but are not strictly comparable. The cohort-dispersion (IQR) monitor from the Private Credit report is omitted: at n=5 with vintages spanning 2012–2023 the statistic is not meaningful; it will be reinstated if the cohort is broadened to PitchBook’s transportation / asset-based benchmark universes. ABS pricing in the funding-cost league is compiled from trade press and rating-agency presales (Ishka, Aviation News, ASR, KBRA, Fitch); paywalled 2026 prints are carried as n.d. and populate next quarter. The 14-Aug-26 screen is archived as the 2026Q3 baseline snapshot.
